title: The Kunz Axe (Votive Were-Jaguar Celt)
originLocation: Oaxaca, Mexico
medium: Carved and polished blue-green jadeite
creator: Unknown Olmec master lapidary
repository: American Museum of Natural History, New York (30/7552)
commonsFile: Kunz axe, Olmec - Mesoamerican objects in the American Museum of Natural History - DSC06013.JPG
anatomy: cleft cranial crown associated with maize and earth fissures
downturned snarling feline mouth with flared nostrils
flame-shaped eyebrows above almond eyes
crouching human infant torso clasping a miniature celt
description: Standing 31 cm tall in translucent blue-green Guatemalan jadeite, the Kunz Axe merges a ritual celt blade with the crouching body of a supernatural human-feline infant. Its deeply notched cranium, flame eyebrows, and snarling jaguar maw epitomize the Olmec 'were-jaguar' rain and earth-fertility spirit, likely buried as an elite dedicatory offering rather than used as a utilitarian tool.

title: Jade Mosaic Mask-Pectoral of the Zapotec Bat God
originLocation: Mound H, Monte Albán, Oaxaca, Mexico
medium: Fitted dark-green jadeite plaques with shell inlays on modeled matrix
creator: Unknown Zapotec royal workshop
repository: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Mexico City
anatomy: erect leaf-shaped nasal crest of a phyllostomid bat
rounded upright chiropteran ears
humanoid jaws baring interlocking shell teeth
suspended jadeite ear-spools and tripartite pendant plaques
description: Excavated in an elite offering beneath Mound H at Monte Albán, this 28 cm funerary pectoral is assembled from twenty-five precision-cut plaques of dark-green jadeite accented with marine shell eyes and teeth. Combining an anthropomorphized fanged visage with the erect nose-leaf and rounded ears of the Mesoamerican leaf-nosed bat, the deity governed night, caves, agricultural fertility, and sacrificial decapitation.

title: Tenoned Stone Head of the Feathered Serpent
originLocation: Temple of the Feathered Serpent (Ciudadela), Teotihuacan, Mexico
medium: Carved volcanic andesite/basalt with traces of stucco and pigment
creator: Unknown Teotihuacan state sculptors
repository: Zona Arqueológica de Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (in situ)
anatomy: radial collar of overlapping quetzal tail-plumes
fanged reptilian jaws with bifurcated snout
undulating rattlesnake body carved along adjacent talud-tablero panels
description: Projecting dramatically from the stepped talud-tablero facade of the Ciudadela pyramid at Teotihuacan, these monumental tenoned stone heads represent the earliest monumental architectural program dedicated to the Mesoamerican Feathered Serpent. Each snarling rattlesnake head emerges from a blossom-like ruff of carved quetzal feathers, alternating along the balustrade with mosaic-like headdresses of a primordial crocodilian war spirit while undulating serpent bodies swim through carved seashells.

title: Polychrome Ceramic Plate of the Underworld Bat (Camazotz)
creature: Killer Bat of the Maya Underworld
originLocation: Balamkú, Campeche, Mexico
medium: Slip-painted polychrome earthenware
creator: Unknown Classic Maya ceramicist
repository: Museo de Arquitectura Maya, Baluarte de la Soledad / Fuerte de San Miguel, Campeche
anatomy: outstretched scalloped chiropteran wing membranes marked with death motifs
upturned leaf-nosed snout and bared fangs
clawed thumbs and talons flanking a skeletal underworld torso
description: Recovered from an elite Classic Maya tomb at Balamkú in Campeche, this slip-painted ceramic tripod plate centers on a nocturnal vampire-bat spirit spreading dark, scalloped wings across a fiery orange-red ground. In Maya myth—later codified in the Popol Vuh as Camazotz, guardian of the House of Bats in Xibalba—such chiropteran wayob spirits acted as nocturnal agents of bloodletting, darkness, and decapitation.

title: Yaxchilan Lintel 25: Lady K'abal Xook Conjuring the Vision Serpent
originLocation: Structure 23, Yaxchilan, Chiapas, Mexico
medium: Carved fine-grained limestone door lintel
creator: Unknown Classic Maya court sculptor of Yaxchilan
repository: The British Museum, London (Am1923, Maud.5)
commonsFile: Yaxchilan (Maya) Lintel 25 Depicting Appearance of Way from Jaws of Vision Serpent (9817557966).jpg
anatomy: towering S-coiled bicephalic serpent body rising from burning blood-soaked paper
gaping upper serpent jaws disgorging an armed ancestral warrior
lower rear serpent head manifesting the rain-war deity Tlaloc
description: Set above the central doorway of Queen Lady K'abal Xook's ritual structure at Yaxchilan, this masterwork of Classic Maya limestone relief captures the climax of a royal bloodletting rite celebrating King Itzamnaaj Bahlam III's accession. From a bowl of burning bark-paper strips saturated with the queen's sacrificial blood coils the double-headed Vision Serpent Waxaklajuun Ubaah Chan, opening its fanged upper jaws tobridge the mortal and supernatural realms as a spear-wielding patron warrior emerges.

title: Stone Sculpture of Xiuhcoatl (The Turquoise Fire Serpent)
originLocation: Tenochtitlan (Mexico City), Basin of Mexico
medium: Carved volcanic basalt
creator: Unknown Mexica imperial sculptor
repository: The British Museum, London (Am1825,1210.19)
anatomy: recurved horn-like snout studded with seven stellar orbs
gaping fanged reptilian jaws and clawed forelimbs
segmented trapezoidal tail terminating in the triangular year-sign and fire-drill rays
description: Carved from dense grey volcanic stone, this Mexica monument embodies Xiuhcoatl, the celestial Turquoise Fire Serpent wielded as a living lightning bolt by the solar war god Huitzilopochtli to slay Coyolxauhqui at Coatepec. Its arched, star-studded snout curves backward above cavernous fangs while its segmented body terminates in the bound A-O solar-year trapeze, uniting meteoric fire, drought, and calendrical renewal.

title: Cipactli, the Primordial Crocodilian Earth Monster (Codex Borgia)
originLocation: Puebla-Tlaxcala Valley or Cholula, Central Mexico
medium: Mineral and organic pigments on gesso-primed deerskin screenfold
creator: Unknown Nahua tlacuilo (painter-scribe)
repository: Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vatican City (Borg. mess. 1)
anatomy: ridge of shark-like dorsal spines along an armored crocodilian back
upper jaw armed with recurved flint-like fangs and no lower jaw
clawed reptilian limbs associated with insatiable joint-mouths
description: Painted on gessoed deerskin in the pre-Conquest divinatory manuscript Codex Borgia, Cipactli presides over the very first day-sign of the 260-day tonalpohualli ritual calendar. In Central Mexican cosmogony, the gods Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca grappled with this voracious caiman-sawfish monster swimming in the primordial waters—tearing its spiny body asunder to fashion the mountains, valleys, and fertile surface of the earth.

title: Turquoise Mosaic Pectoral of a Double-Headed Serpent
originLocation: Puebla-Oaxaca or Tenochtitlan, Mexico
medium: Turquoise, spiny oyster (Spondylus), and conch shell mosaic on carved Spanish cedar wood
creator: Unknown Mixtec-Nahua master lapidary-mosaicist
repository: The British Museum, London (Am1894,-.634)
commonsFile: Turquoise Mosaic of a Double-Headed Serpent (Mixtec-Aztec, AD 1400-1521) - British Museum.jpg
anatomy: symmetrical undulating body encrusted with roughly two thousand turquoise tesserae
twin opposing serpent heads baring white conch-shell fangs
crimson Spondylus shell gums and nostrils once paired with iron-pyrite eyes
description: Carved from a single block of fragrant Cedrela odorata wood and encrusted with nearly two thousand tesserae of turquoise imported from the American Southwest, this 43 cm pectoral is among the supreme surviving works of Mesoamerican lapidary regalia. Its twin snarling heads—trimmed in crimson thorny oyster and white strombus shell—evoke Maquizcoatl, the ominous double-headed serpent of Aztec sky-portents and priestly Renewal ceremonies, and may have formed part of Moctezuma II's diplomatic treasure sent to Europe in 1519.

title: Coiled Feathered Serpent (Quetzalcoatl)
originLocation: Central Mexico
medium: Carved volcanic basalt
creator: Unknown Mexica sculptor
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (00.5.32)
anatomy: tightly wound muscular coils covered in layered avian plumage
flared supraorbital brow scales over sunken eyes
extruded bifurcated serpent tongue and segmented tail rattles
description: Sculpted in the round—including finely incised ventral scales on its underside—this compact volcanic basalt monument fuses the lethal terrestrial power of the Mesoamerican rattlesnake with the iridescent sky-plumage of the resplendent quetzal. Coiled in potent equilibrium with its forked tongue flicking beneath heavy feathered brows, the sculpture embodies Quetzalcoatl as wind-bringer, morning star, and divine patron of Mexica priesthood and kingship.

title: Carved Relief Plaque of the Ahuizotl from Tepoztlán
originLocation: Tepoztlán, Morelos, Mexico
medium: Carved volcanic stone relief
creator: Unknown Mexica imperial sculptor
repository: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Mexico City
commonsFile: Lápida de Ahuízotl - octavo Huey Tlatoani de los mexicas.jpg
anatomy: lithe otter- or dog-like quadrupedal body surrounded by stylized water-scrolls
monkey-like clawed paws and pointed canine ears
long prehensile tail terminating in a dextrous human hand
description: Originally adorning a sacred temple structure at Tepoztlán, this crisp stone relief serves simultaneously as the royal name-glyph of the eighth Mexica Huey Tlatoani, Ahuitzotl (r. 1486–1502), and as a portrait of his namesake lake monster. Feared by fishermen of Lake Texcoco and vividly described in Book XI of the Florentine Codex, the amphibious Ahuizotl lurked in deep whirlpools as servant of the rain gods Tlaloc and Chalchiuhtlicue, luring victims with infant-like cries before dragging them underwater with the human hand at the tip of its tail.

title: The Raimondi Stela (Composite Staff Deity)
originLocation: Chavín de Huántar, Ancash Highlands, Peru
medium: Polished and incised light-grey granite monolith
creator: Unknown Chavín temple sculptor
repository: Museo Nacional de Arqueología, Antropología e Historia del Perú, Lima
anatomy: snarling jaguar-caiman mouth with crossed saber fangs
raptor talons on hands and feet gripping elaborate serpentiform staffs
towering anatropic headdress of stacked feline and caiman jaws sprouting serpent hair
description: Standing nearly two meters high in polished granite, the Raimondi Stela employs ingenious contour rivalry (anatropic double-reading) to portray the supreme composite deity of the Early Horizon Andes. Viewed upright, a squat jaguar-mouthed, talon-footed figure clutches two baroque ceremonial staffs beneath a headdress twice its own height; inverted, that towering crown transforms into a cascading column of nested smiling caiman-feline maws fringed with writhing serpents.

title: Funerary Mantle Fragment with the Flying Oculate Being
originLocation: Carhua(?), Ica / South Coast of Peru
medium: Pigment-painted plain-weave cotton textile
creator: Unknown Paracas textile artist
repository: The Cleveland Museum of Art (2005.19)
commonsFile: Peru, South Coast, Paracas (700 BC - 1 AD), Carhua? - Fragment of a Mantle with Oculate Being - 2005.19 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
anatomy: enormous concentric staring discs encircling the eyes
elongated upturned nose and wide toothy smile
floating horizontal body trailing serrated serpentiform streamers and trophy heads
description: Preserved by the hyper-arid sands of Peru's southern desert coast, this painted cotton burial-bundle fragment depicts the enigmatic 'Oculate Being' hovering weightlessly in ecstatic flight. Characterized by hypnotic concentric eyes, a wide grinning mouth, and sinuous barbed appendages radiating from its head and torso, this supernatural spirit mediated soul-flight, agricultural regeneration, and ancestral transformation between Paracas mummy bundles and the mythic world.

title: Polychrome Double-Spout Bottle of the Mythical Killer Whale
originLocation: Ica / Rio Grande de Nazca Valley, South Coast of Peru
medium: Polychrome slip-painted burnished earthenware
creator: Unknown Nazca master potter
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (64.228.70)
commonsFile: Double Spout Bottle, Killer Whale MET 64.228.70 d.jpg
anatomy: crescentic cetacean body with prominent dorsal fin and bilobed tail fluke
fanged jaws smeared with sacrificial blood
extended human forelimb capable of clutching knives or severed trophy heads
description: Modeled and painted in glossy mineral slips around a globular double-spout-and-bridge bottle, the Mythical Killer Whale (Orca Mítica) ranks as the supreme marine predator deity of Nazca iconography. Merging the sleek piebald body and dorsal fin of Orcinus orca with terrifying serrated jaws and a human arm, the creature personified oceanic power, maritime abundance, and ritual head-taking across the southern Peruvian coast—where its colossal form was also etched into the Nazca desert pampa.

title: Polychrome Temple Frieze of Ai Apaec ('The Decapitator')
originLocation: Huaca de la Luna, Moche Valley, La Libertad, Peru
medium: Molded adobe high-relief mural painted in mineral red, yellow, white, and black pigments
creator: Unknown Moche temple muralists
repository: Complejo Arqueológico Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, Trujillo, Peru (in situ)
anatomy: wrinkled anthropoid visage with bulging eyes and interlocking jaguar fangs
radiating arachnid or octopoid appendages terminating in snarling zoomorphic heads
ceremonial tumi sacrificial knife and severed human head held in opposing hands
description: Conserved across the stepped adobe courtyard facades of Huaca de la Luna near Trujillo, this vivid polychrome relief depicts the fearsome Moche supernatural known to archaeologists as 'The Decapitator' (Ai Apaec). Combining the crossed fangs of an Andean jaguar with the ensnaring legs of a trapdoor spider or sea monster, the deity brandishes a crescent blade and a severed trophy head by the hair, presiding over warrior capture sacrifices intended to appease mountain and storm forces.

title: Gold Ceremonial Knife (Tumi) Surmounted by Winged Naylamp
originLocation: Batán Grande / Lambayeque Valley, North Coast of Peru
medium: Hammered, repoussé, and lost-wax cast gold alloy with crushed turquoise inlay
creator: Unknown Sicán court goldsmith
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1979.206.1247)
anatomy: sprouting avian wings flanking the shoulders
characteristic comma-shaped upturned avian eyes
monumental semicircular filigree headdress inlaid with turquoise
description: Rising above a crescentic sacrificial blade, the handle of this Middle Sicán gold tumi portrays the winged founder-deity traditionally identified with Ñaymlap—the legendary maritime ruler who arrived on balsa rafts in the Lambayeque Valley and ultimately sprouted wings to fly heavenward rather than suffer mortal death. Executed in shimmering sheet gold with suspended spangles and turquoise inlays, the figure's comma-shaped bird eyes and feathered pinions embody divine royal ancestry.

title: Gold Masked Figure Pendant of the Tairona Bat-Man
originLocation: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Magdalena, Colombia
medium: Lost-wax cast tumbaga (gold-copper alloy) with surface depletion gilding
creator: Unknown Tairona master goldsmith
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1991.419.31)
anatomy: upturned leaf-nosed bat visor and fanged chiropteran muzzle
twin soaring frigatebird or macaw heads flanking an openwork braided headdress
human torso grasping double-ended ceremonial serpent bars
description: Cast by the lost-wax process in high-karat depletion-gilded tumbaga, this intricate pectoral pendant portrays a Tairona priest-cacique in full ontological transformation into the mythical Hombre-Murciélago ('Bat-Man'). Crowned by twin sacred birds and wearing a tubular nose ornament, lip plug, and leaf-nosed bat snout, the nocturnal winged intermediary bridges the dark subterranean underworld of caves with the sunlit peaks of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.

title: Engraved Marine Shell Gorget of the Supernatural Rattlesnake
creature: Horned / Plumed Rattlesnake of the Beneath World
originLocation: Moundville / Tennessee-Cumberland Valley region, Southeastern United States
medium: Carved, fenestrated, and incised lightning whelk shell (Sinistrofulgur perversum)
creator: Unknown Mississippian shell engraver
repository: Alabama Museum of Natural History, Tuscaloosa
anatomy: coiled cross-hatched diamondback body encircling an openwork central head
cosmological cross-in-circle motif framing the supernatural eye
gaping fanged mouth and segmented tail rattle along the outer rim
description: Cut from the outer whorl of a Gulf Coast marine whelk shell and worn suspended at the throat as high-status regalia, this Mississippian gorget coils a supernatural rattlesnake around its own snarling head. Marked with concentric chevron bands, fenestrated cutouts, and a sacred cross-in-circle eye, the Great Serpent reigned over the watery Beneath World in Southeastern Indigenous cosmology while conferring war medicine, storm power, and renewal.

title: Ceramic Effigy Bowl of the Underwater Panther
originLocation: Rhodes Place, Crittenden County, Arkansas, United States
medium: Modeled, incised, and burnished shell-tempered dark earthenware
creator: Unknown Late Mississippian ceramic artist
repository: National Museum of the American Indian, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. / New York
anatomy: sculpted cougar head rising from the vessel rim with bared fangs and horns
swirling incised scroll-bands representing whirlpools and scales across the body
elongated serpentine tail curving around the opposite rim lug
description: Unearthed at the Late Mississippian mound center of Rhodes Place in the Central Mississippi Valley, this polished dark-ware effigy vessel embodies the dread lord of the subaqueous realm: the Underwater Panther. Combining the horned, snarling head of a mountain lion with a long serpent tail and incised vortex scrolls, the chimeric beast governed rivers, whirlpools, and healing medicine in eternal cosmic tension with the Thunderbirds of the Upper World.

title: Agawa Rock Cliff Pictograph of Mishipeshu (The Great Lynx)
originLocation: Agawa Rock, Lake Superior, Ontario, Canada
medium: Red iron-oxide ochre mixed with fish-oil binder on sheer granite cliff face
creator: Attributed in Anishinaabe oral history to the warrior-leader Myeengun
repository: Lake Superior Provincial Park, Ontario, Canada (in situ)
anatomy: twin curved horns crowning a feline head
sawtooth ridge of dragon-like spines along back and tail
flanking giant horned water-serpents below an Ojibwe canoe flotilla
description: Painted in red ochre on a sheer granite ledge just above the crashing waves of eastern Lake Superior, the Agawa Rock panel is the most celebrated surviving depiction of Mishibizhiw, the Great Underwater Lynx of Algonquian and Anishinaabe tradition. Guarding Lake Superior's submerged copper deposits and capable of whipping calm waters into sudden tempests with its spiny tail, the horned feline spirit accompanies twin giant serpents and canoes commemorating a perilous cross-lake expedition led by the shaman-chief Myeengun.

title: Ceremonial Dantsikw Power Boards Depicting the Sisiutl
originLocation: Northern Vancouver Island / Queen Charlotte Strait, British Columbia, Canada
medium: Carved and polychrome-painted red cedar wood
creator: Unknown 19th-century Kwakwaka'wakw carver
repository: Ethnologisches Museum, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
anatomy: opposing horned serpent heads with curled tongues at either extremity
central frontal humanoid face with upturned horns
formline-painted scales imbued with petrifying warrior medicine
description: Collected on the Northwest Coast in 1881 by Johan Adrian Jacobsen for Berlin's Ethnological Museum, these painted wooden dantsikw boards manifest the formidable supernatural power of Sisiutl, the bicephalic horned sea-serpent of Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonialism. Flanking a central horned human visage with two outward-facing fanged dragon heads, the amphibious Sisiutl could transform into a self-propelled canoe, turn the unprepared to stone with its gaze, and render warriors invulnerable when its blood bathed their skin.

title: 'Namgis Thunderbird Transformation Mask
originLocation: Alert Bay / Cormorant Island region, British Columbia, Canada
medium: Carved red cedar wood, mineral and commercial pigments, leather hinges, metal, and cordage
creator: Unknown 19th-century 'Namgis (Kwakwaka'wakw) master carver
repository: Brooklyn Museum, New York (08.491.8902)
commonsFile: Namgis (Native American). Thunderbird Transformation Mask, 19th century.jpg
anatomy: massive hooked raptor beak split vertically along hidden rigging cords
curling supernatural horn-crest feathers atop the head
hinged outer avian halves opening wide to reveal an ancestral human face within
description: Acquired in British Columbia during Stewart Culin's early museum expeditions, this kinetic 'Namgis transformation mask dramatizes the foundational Kwakwaka'wakw myth in which the celestial Thunderbird descended to earth and shed its avian cloak to become a clan ancestor. Operated by concealed pull-strings in the firelight of the winter tseka ceremonial house, the hooked eagle-like beak and painted wings swing dramatically apart—flashing lightning from its eyes and booming thunder with its pinions—to reveal the human face inside.

title: Copper and Abalone Crest Mask of the Sea Bear
creature: Haida Sea Bear / Oceanic Predator Monster
originLocation: Haida Gwaii, British Columbia, Canada
medium: Hammered native/trade sheet copper inlaid with Haliotis abalone shell and fur trim
creator: Unknown 19th-century Haida metalworker
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1979.206.830)
anatomy: broad ursine snout and flared nostrils repoussé-worked in lustrous copper
iridescent abalone-shell irises and bared predatory teeth
amphibious marine ears and sea-mammal fur crest
description: Hammered from prestigious sheet copper—the ultimate emblem of aristocratic wealth along the Pacific Northwest Coast—this rare Haida mask portrays the supernatural Sea Bear, cousin to the sea-wolf Wasgo (Gonakadet) that inhabits the abyssal trenches off Haida Gwaii. In flickering firelight, its iridescent abalone-shell eyes and teeth flash from the burnished copper surface, embodying the amphibious ocean spirits whose underwater houses mirrored chiefdom lineages ashore.

title: Carved Marine Ivory Tupilaq (Avenging Spirit Monster)
originLocation: East / West Greenland
medium: Carved sperm-whale tooth or walrus tusk ivory
creator: Unknown Kalaallit (East Greenlandic) carver
repository: Nunatta Katersugaasivia Allagaateqarfialu (Greenland National Museum and Archives), Nuuk
anatomy: grotesque grimacing head with hollowed sockets and bared teeth
exposed skeletal ribcage fused with seal, bird, and human limbs
compact hand-held form carved to materialize an invisible shamanic construct
description: In traditional Kalaallit belief, a tupilaq was a perishable avenging monster secretly assembled by a sorcerer from mismatched animal bones, sinew, peat, and hide, brought to life through chant, and launched into the icy sea to hunt down a rival—though a stronger shaman could turn the creature back to devour its maker. Because real ritual tupilait were never seen by uninitiated eyes, late 19th-century East Greenlanders carved dense walrus and whale ivory sculptures like this specimen to show early ethnographers what the terrifying spirit-chimeras looked like.

title: Hamatsa Masks of Crooked Beak of Heaven (Galokwudzuwis) and Hokhokw
originLocation: Alert Bay, Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada
medium: Carved and painted red cedar wood, shredded red cedar bark, eagle feathers, and cordage
creator: Yakuglas (Charlie James, c. 1867–1938)
repository: Portland Art Museum, Oregon
commonsFile: Crooked beak mask and Huxwhukw mask, by Yakuglas Charlie James (1875-1938), Kwakwka'wakw, c. 1900, red cedar, red cedar bark, feathers, paint, string - Portland Art Museum - Portland, Oregon - DSC09113.jpg
anatomy: extravagantly curved and scrolled upper beak of Galokwudzuwis
elongated crane-like skull-cracking beak of Huxwhukw
hinged clapping lower mandibles framed by blood-red shredded cedar bark
description: Carved around 1900 by the renowned Kwakwaka'wakw master Yakuglas (Charlie James), this dramatic pair of articulated cedar masks embodies two monstrous avian attendants of Baxwbakwalanuksiwe' ('Man-Eater at the North End of the World') in the sacred Hamatsa winter initiation dance. Draped in dyed-red cedar bark and manipulated with hidden cords so their massive wooden mandibles snap thunderously in rhythm with the drums, Huxwhukw cracks human skulls with its lance-like bill while Galokwudzuwis ('Crooked Beak of Heaven') devours flesh from the sky realm.

title: Orongo Basalt Petroglyphs of the Tangata Manu (Birdman)
originLocation: Mata Ngarau, Orongo Ceremonial Village, Rano Kau, Rapa Nui (Easter Island)
medium: Bas-relief pecked and abraded volcanic basalt
creator: Unknown Rapa Nui rongorongo / ritual carvers
repository: Rapa Nui National Park, Chile (in situ)
commonsFile: PETROGLYPHS ON THE ROCKS NEAR ORONGO VILLAGE - EASTER ISLAND.jpg
anatomy: long hooked beak and gular throat pouch of the great frigatebird (makohe)
crouched anthropomorphic torso with arched spine and flexed knees
humanoid hand often cradling the sacred first sooty-tern egg (manutara)
description: Carved in dense clusters across the sea-cliff basalt boulders of Mata Ngarau on the rim of Rano Kau volcano, hundreds of bas-relief Tangata Manu figures commemorate victors of Rapa Nui's annual Birdman competition in honor of the creator god Make-Make. Blending a crouched human athlete's body with the hooked bill of a frigatebird, each relief immortalized the sacred ruler whose swimmer retrieved the season's first manutara egg from the offshore islet of Motu Nui.

title: Carved Meeting-House Doorway Lintel (Pare) Flanked by Manaia
originLocation: Bay of Plenty / East Coast, North Island, Aotearoa (New Zealand)
medium: Openwork carved tōtara wood (Podocarpus totara) inlaid with pāua (Haliotis iris) shell
creator: Unknown 19th-century Māori tohunga whakairo (master carver)
repository: The Cleveland Museum of Art (1962.350)
commonsFile: Unknown artist - Lintel (Pare) - 1962.350 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
anatomy: strict profile head terminating in a curved bird-like beak
contorted serpentine torso woven through openwork takarangi spirals
three-fingered avian-reptilian claws and luminous pāua-shell eye
description: Mounted above the threshold of an ancestral wharenui to mark the perilous transition between the tapu realm inside and the everyday world outside, this openwork tōtara pare lintel flanks a central ancestral figure with two outward-facing manaia guardians. Always rendered in profile with a curved beak, glowing pāua eye, and three-taloned hands, the manaia acts across Māori woodcarving as an unseen messenger and protective spiritual counterpart bridging sky, sea, and human lineages.

title: Malagan Ceremonial Mask of an Ancestral Bush and Sea Spirit
originLocation: New Ireland, Bismarck Archipelago, Papua New Guinea
medium: Carved Alstonia wood, lime, red ochre, charcoal pigment, plant fiber, and Turbo petholatus shell opercula
creator: Unknown 19th-century New Ireland master carver
repository: Etnografiska museet, Stockholm
commonsFile: Malagan funeral mask, New Ireland, Papua New Guinea, 1887 - Etnografiska museet - Stockholm, Sweden - DSC00940.JPG
anatomy: hypnotic green-eyed gaze formed from sea-snail shell opercula (Turbo petholatus)
pierced openwork lateral ear-flanges intertwining avian and serpent motifs
fierce fanged grimace crowned by a sculpted fiber crest
description: Collected in northern New Ireland in 1887, this polychrome openwork wooden mask belonged to the culminating malagan mortuary cycle that liberated the spirits of the dead from the world of the living while transferring clan land and ritual copyrights. Set with luminous sea-snail operculum eyes and flanked by pierced wings of intertwined birds, snakes, and bush spirits (ruruh), such carvings served briefly as living skin-vessels for ancestral life-force before being ritually destroyed or relinquished.

title: Carved Amo Post of the Sea-Taniwha Marakihau at Wairaka Wharenui
originLocation: Wairaka Marae, Whakatāne, Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa (New Zealand)
medium: Relief-carved tōtara wood architectural upright (amo); historic glass-plate negative
creator: Teira Te Ngarara and Wepiha Apanui (Ngāti Awa master carvers)
repository: Wairaka Marae, Whakatāne (archival image: Alexander Turnbull Library, Wellington, 1/2-019091-G)
commonsFile: Exterior view of Wairaka Meeting House, Whakatane, showing the marakihau (mermaid) carving on the left amo ATLIB 291936.png
anatomy: humanoid upper torso and horned head adorned with spiral surface patterning
long coiled fish tail replacing the lower limbs
hollow funnel-like tubular tongue (ngongo) sucking in fish and canoes
description: Carved in the 1890s by Ngāti Awa masters Teira Te Ngarara and Wepiha Apanui for the front porch upright (amo) of Wairaka meeting house in Whakatāne, this renowned panel portrays a marakihau—a formidable marine taniwha of eastern Bay of Plenty tradition. Sporting a sinuous coiled fish tail, horned brow, and an elongated hollow funnel-tongue (ngongo), the ocean guardian could inhale entire schools of fish or draw passing waka canoes down into submarine caverns.

title: Arnhem Land Ochre Rock Painting of the Rainbow Serpent
originLocation: Western Arnhem Land escarpment, Northern Territory, Australia
dateDisplay: Pre-contact Dreaming rock art tradition (c. 2000 BCE–1500 CE)
medium: Natural red and white earth-ochre pigments on sandstone rock-shelter wall
creator: Unknown ancestral Arnhem Land rock-shelter artist

description: Painted in iron-rich red ochre across a sheltered sandstone overhang in Northern Australia, this ancestral rock painting depicts the Rainbow Serpent—known in Western Arnhem Land Kunwinjku traditions as Ngalyod or the creator-mother Yingarna. Emerging at the end of the Ice Age in Arnhem Land's rock-art sequence, this colossal composite python-macropod spirit carved river gorges, dwells in permanent billabongs, unleashes regenerative monsoonal storms, and swallows rule-breakers who disturb sacred waters.

description: Sheltered beneath the sandstone cliffs of Burrunggui (Nourlangie) in Kakadu, these delicate red-ochre figures depict the Mimi—ancient fairy-like spirits of the Arnhem Land plateau who first taught Aboriginal ancestors how to hunt kangaroo, cook with fire, dance, and paint rock walls before humans arrived. Because their bodies are as slender as blades of grass and would snap in a stiff breeze, the Mimi blow open hairline fissures in the sandstone escarpment to live deep inside the rock, emerging only on windless nights.
